# Exercise 1
The number of patients with cancer among \(150\) patients has a binomial distribution,
\(X\sim B(150,0.007)\). This distribution can be approximated by a Poisson distribution,
\(Y\sim Pois(150\times 0.007)\).

`(i)` 
```{r}
dbinom(0,150,0.007)
dpois(0,150*0.007)
```   

`(ii)` 
\(\Pr[X>2] = 1-\Pr[X\le2]\) and the same for \(Y\), hence
```{r}
1-pbinom(2,150,0.007)
1-ppois(2,150*0.007)
```   

# Exercise 2
The number of pages with typos has a binomial distribution,
\(X\sim B(32625,0.0005)\). 
\(\Pr[X\ge 14] = 1-\Pr[X < 14] = 1-\Pr[X\le13] =\)
```{r}
1-pbinom(13,32625,0.0005)
```  
Or we could use the Poisson approximation, which is very precise in this case:
```{r}
1-ppois(13,32625*0.0005)
```   

# Exercises 3 
Let \(X\) be the ozone concentration (ozone level), \(X\sim{N}(12,3^2)\).

## a)
`(i)` \(\Pr[X<10]=\Pr[X\le 10]\approx\)
```{r}
pnorm(10,12,3)
```   

`(ii)` \(\Pr[X<14]\approx\)
```{r}
pnorm(14,12,3)
```   

`(iii)` \(\Pr[X<16]\approx\)
```{r}
pnorm(16,12,3)
```   

`(iv)` \(\Pr[X>10]=\Pr[X\ge 10]\approx\)
```{r}
1-pnorm(10,12,3)
```   
Note that \(10\) and \(14\) are symmetric around the mean, hence \(\Pr[X>10]=\Pr[X<14]\).

`(v)` \(\Pr[X>9]\approx\)
```{r}
1-pnorm(9,12,3)
```   

`(vi)` \(\Pr[9<X<11]=\Pr[X<11]-\Pr[X\le9]=\Pr[X<11]-\Pr[X<9]\approx\)
```{r}
pnorm(11,12,3)-pnorm(9,12,3)
```   

`(vii)` \(\Pr[11<X<14]\approx\)
```{r}
pnorm(14,12,3)-pnorm(11,12,3)
```   

## b)
The first quartile is \(x^*_{0.25}\) such that \(\Pr[X \le x^*_{0.25}] = 0.25\), hence \(x^*_{0.25}\approx\)
```{r}
qnorm(0.25,12,3)
```   
The \(95^\text{th}\) percentile is \(x^*_{0.95}\) such that \(\Pr[X \le x^*_{0.95}] = 0.95\), hence \(x^*_{0.95}\approx\)
```{r}
qnorm(0.95,12,3)
```   

# Exercise 4
Let $X$ be the life span of a shrub. $X\sim{N}(6,2^2)$

## a)
`(i)` $\Pr[X\le8] =$
```{r}
pnorm(8,6,2)
```
`(ii)` $\Pr[X>8] =$
```{r}
pnorm(8,6,2,FALSE)
```
`(iii)` $\Pr[6 \le X \le 8] = \Pr[X\le8] - \Pr[X\le6] =$
```{r}
pnorm(8,6,2)-pnorm(6,6,2)
```
`(iv)` $\Pr[X\le0] =$
```{r}
pnorm(0,6,2)
```
This probability is small, but non-zero, which does not make sense for real shrubs. 
The reason is that modelling bounded values as the life span by normal distribution is possible only near their average value.

## b)
The life span $x_{>,0.25}$ exceeded by $25$% of the population is the value such that $\Pr[X \ge x_{>,0.25}]=0.25$:
```{r}
qnorm(0.25,6,2,FALSE)
```
That is, $25$% of the shrubs live $7.3$ years or more.

The life span $x_{>,0.75}$ exceeded by $75$% of the population is the value such that $\Pr[X \ge x_{>,0.75}]=0.75$:
```{r}
qnorm(0.75,6,2,FALSE)
```

# Exercise 5
$X\sim{N}(450,100^2)$ is the score of one randomly selected person.  

## a)
$\Pr[400 < X < 500] = \Pr[X<500] - \Pr[X<400] =$
```{r}
pnorm(500,450,100) - pnorm(400,450,100)
```  
## b)
$\Pr[X>480] =$
```{r}
pnorm(480,450,100,lower.tail=FALSE)
```  
## c)  
We need to find $x^*$ such that $\Pr[X>x^*]\le0.1$
```{r}
qnorm(0.1,450,100,lower.tail=FALSE)
```  
To get an integer score, we must round up to $579$ (note that a normal distribution cannot be a fully adequate model for integer scores).   

## d) 
Let the individual scores be \(X_i\sim{N}(450,100^2)\), \(i=1,\ldots,20\).
This is a random group, so the scores are independent.
Their average score is \(\bar X = \frac{1}{20}\sum_{i=1}^{20} X_i\),
and the distribution of it is normal.

`(i)` 
\(\mathbf{E} \bar X = 450\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=100^2/20=500\),
hence the standard deviation of the average is \(\sqrt{500}\approx22.36\).

`(ii)`
\(\bar X\sim{N}(450,100^2/20)\) and 
\(\Pr[\bar X\ge 480]=1-\Pr[\bar X\le 480]\approx\)
```{r}
1-pnorm(480,450,sqrt(500))
```   

`(iii)`
\(\Pr[\text{for all } i\:X_i<480] = \Pr[X_1\le 480]\cdot\Pr[X_2\le 480]\cdots\Pr[X_{20}\le 480]
       = {\bigl(\Pr[X_i\le 480]\bigr)^{20}}\approx\)
```{r}
format((pnorm(480,450,100))^20,scientific=FALSE)
```   

`(iv)`
\(\Pr[\text{there is } i\text{ such that }X_i<480] = 1 - \Pr[\text{for all } i\:X_i\ge 480]\approx\)
```{r}
print(1-(1-pnorm(480,450,100))^20,digits=10)
```   


# Exercise 6
Let \(X\) be the weight of a bag, \(X\sim{N}(25,0.5^2)\).

## a)
`(i)` \(\Pr[X>25]=0.5\)

`(ii)` \(\Pr[24<X<26]\approx\)
```{r}
pnorm(26,25,0.5)-pnorm(24,25,0.5)
```    

## b)
The weights of each bag are \(X_i\sim{N}(25,0.5^2)\), \(i=1,\ldots,100\), 
and as they are independent,
\(S=\sum_{i=1}^{100} X_i\sim{N}(25\cdot100,0.5^2\cdot100)\).

\(\Pr[2400<S<2600] = \Pr[S \le 2600] - \Pr[S \le 2400] \approx\)
```{r}
pnorm(2600,2500,5)-pnorm(2400,2500,5)
```   


# Exercise 7
Let the mean filling weight be $\mu$,
then the weight of a randomly chosen container is $X\sim{N}(\mu,0.6^2)$ and $(X-\mu)/0.6\sim{N}(0,1)$.   
We know that $\Pr[X < 18]=0.02$, hence $\Pr[(X-\mu)/0.6 < (18-\mu)/0.6]=0.02$
and thus $(18-\mu)/0.6 = z^*_{0.02}$,
where $z^*_{0.02}$ is a value such that $\Pr[Z \le z^*_{0.02}]=0.02$.
Finally, $\mu = 18 - 0.6\cdot z^*_{0.02} =$
```{r}
18-0.6*qnorm(0.02)
```  

# Exercise 8

From the symmetry of the probability density function of the normal distribution, 
we get that the mean \(\mu = (15.41 + 15.15)/2 = 15.28\) 
(here we use that both tails, below \(15.15\) and above \(15.41\), have the same probability of \(14\)\%).
  
If \(X\) is the mass of a randomly chosen bird, then \(\frac{X-15.28}{\sigma}\sim{N}(0,1)\),
where \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the mass.
Thus, \((15.15-15.28)/\sigma = z^*_{0.14}\approx\) 
```{r}
qnorm(0.14)
```   
and \(\sigma = (15.15-15.28)/z^*_{0.14} \approx\)
```{r}
(15.15-15.28)/qnorm(0.14)
```   


# Exercise 9   

Let \(X\) be the diameter of a randomly chosen apple, \(X\sim{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\).

From the stated properties, we get two equations, \((85-\mu)/\sigma = z^*_{0.95}\) and 
\((80-\mu)/\sigma = z^*_{0.8}\).

Solving these simultaneous equations, we get
\(\mu = (80\cdot z^*_{0.95} - 85\cdot z^*_{0.8})/(z^*_{0.95} - z^*_{0.8}) \approx\)
```{r}
(80*qnorm(0.95) - 85*qnorm(0.8))/(qnorm(0.95) - qnorm(0.8))
```   
and \(\sigma = (85-80)/(z^*_{0.95}-z^*_{0.8}) \approx\)
```{r}
(85 - 80)/(qnorm(0.95) - qnorm(0.8))
```   


# Exercise 10
Let \(X\) be the income of a randomly chosen UK taxpayer. \(\mathbf{E} X=27\,300\) pounds. 
Note that we have no reasons to assume that \(X\) has a normal distribution.

## a)
By the Law of Large Numbers with \(n=1\) and \(\varepsilon=6\,300\), we have
\(\Pr[|X-27\,300|\ge6\,300]\le\frac{\mathrm{Var}(X)}{(6\,300)^2}\).
As \(\Pr[|X-27\,300|\ge6\,300] = \Pr[X\ge 33\,600] + \Pr[X\le 21\,000]= 0.285 + 0.5 = 0.785\),
we get \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)} \ge 6\,300\sqrt{0.785} \approx 5\,581.81\)

## b)
Similarly to the previous item,
\(\Pr[|X-27\,300|\ge 122\,700]\le\frac{\mathrm{Var}(X)}{(122\,700)^2}\).

As \(\Pr[|X-27\,300|\ge 122\,700] = \Pr[X\ge 150\,000] + \Pr[X\le -95\,400]=0.01\) (negative incomes are impossible),
we get \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)} \ge 122\,700\sqrt{0.01} = 12\,270\).

# Exercise 11
Let $\mu$ be the mean and $\sigma$ the standard deviation of the distribution.  
Let $\bar X_n$ be the sample mean of a random sample of size $n$.

## a) 
$\Pr[|\bar X_{100}-\mu|<\sigma]=1-\Pr[|\bar X_{100}-\mu|\ge\sigma]$.
By the law of large numbers, $\Pr[|\bar X_{100}-\mu|\ge\sigma]\le\frac{\sigma^2}{100\sigma^2}=0.01$, hence
$\Pr[|\bar X_{100}-\mu|<\sigma]\ge0.99$.

## b)
Let $n$ be the required sample size. 
We need to guarantee that $\Pr[|\bar X_n-\mu|<2\sigma]\ge0.99$, 
or equivalently, 
guarantee that $\Pr[|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge2\sigma] = 1-\Pr[|\bar X_n-\mu|<2\sigma] \le 1- 0.99 = 0.01$.
By the law of large numbers, 
$\Pr[|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge 2\sigma]\le\frac{\sigma^2}{n(2\sigma)^2}=\frac{1}{4n}$, hence
it is sufficient if $\frac{1}{4n} \le 0.01$, or $n\ge 25$.

# Exercise 12 

Let \(X\) be the number of Heads in the \(1000\) tossings. 
Let \(Y_i\) be the result of the \(i\)-th tossing, \(Y_i=1\) if a Head occured and \(Y_i=0\) otherwise,
thus \(X = \sum_{i=1}^{1000} Y_i\). 
  
As the number of tossings is large (\(1000\)), we can use the Central Limit Theorem,
and \(\bar Y = \frac{1}{1000}\sum_{i=1}^{1000} Y_i\) has approximately normal distribution
with mean \(0.4\) and variance \(\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{1000}\) (using the mean and variance for a binomial distribution and properties of mean and variance of a sample mean); therefore, 
\(X = 1000 \bar Y\sim {N}(400,240)\).
  
We need to find the smallest \(k\) such that \(\Pr[|X - 400|\ge k] \le 0.05\).
\(\Pr[|X - 400|\ge k] = 2\Pr[X-400 \le -k]\), thus \(-k\) is the \(0.025\)-quantile of \({N}(0,240)\),
and \(k=\)
```{r}
-qnorm(0.025,mean=0,sd=sqrt(240))
```    

# Exercise 13

Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be the random sample, \(\mathbf{E} X_i=\mu\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=3^2\).
Let \(\bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\). 

First assume that \(n\) is large enough to use the Central Limit Theorem
(we will check whether the assumption is correct when we have obtained the value of \(n\));
then \(\bar X_n \sim {N}\left(\mu,\frac{3^2}{n}\right)\), 
hence
\({\Pr[|\bar X_n - \mu|<0.3]} 
    = 
    {\Pr\left[\left|\frac{\bar X_n - \mu}{3/\sqrt{n}}\right|<\frac{0.3}{3/\sqrt{n}}\right]}
    =
    {1-2\Pr\left[\frac{\bar X_n - \mu}{3/\sqrt{n}} < -\frac{0.3}{3/\sqrt{n}}\right]}
\).

As \(1-2\alpha \ge 0.95\) implies that \(\alpha \le 0.025\), we get
\(\quad -\frac{0.3}{3/\sqrt{n}} < z^*_{0.025}\), where \(z^*_{0.025}\) is
the \(0.025\)-quantile of the standard normal distribution.
Therefore, \(n > \left(\frac{-3z^*_{0.025}}{0.3}\right)^2 \approx\)
```{r}
(-3*qnorm(0.025)/0.3)^2
```    
  
The smallest value of \(n\) is \(385\), and this value is large enough to justify the use of the CLT above.

# Exercise 14
Let \(Y_i\) be the result of the \(i\)-th tossing
and the proportion of heads is \(\bar Y_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\).
  
First assume that \(n\) is large enough to apply the Central Limit Theorem.
Then \(\bar Y_n \sim {N}\left(0.4,\frac{0.4\cdot 0.6}{n}\right)\) 
and \(\frac{(\bar Y_n - 0.4)\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}} \sim {N}(0,1)\).
  
### (i)

 \(0.95\le \Pr[0.3\le\bar Y_n\le0.5] 
  = \Pr\left[\frac{-0.1\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}} 
           \le \frac{(\bar Y_n - 0.4)\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}} 
          \le \frac{0.1\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\right]
  = 1-2\Pr\left[\frac{(\bar Y_n - 0.4)\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\le\frac{-0.1\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\right]\), 
thus \(\frac{-0.1\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\le z^*_{0.025}\) and
\(n\ge\left(-10 z^*_{0.025}\sqrt{0.24}\right)^2 \approx\) 
```{r}
(-10*qnorm(0.025)*sqrt(0.24))^2
```   
The smallest value of \(n\) is \(93\), which is large enough for the CLT.

### (ii)
\(0.95\le \Pr[\bar Y_n\le0.5] 
       = \Pr\left[\frac{(\bar Y_n - 0.4)\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\le\frac{0.1\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\right]\), 
thus \(\frac{0.1\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\ge z^*_{0.95}\)
and \(n\ge\left(10 z^*_{0.95}\sqrt{0.24}\right)^2 \approx\)
```{r}
(10*qnorm(0.95)*sqrt(0.24))^2
```   
The smallest value of \(n\) is \(65\), which is probably large enough for the CLT.
            
### (iii)            
\(0.95\le \Pr[\bar Y_n\ge0.2] 
       = \Pr\left[\frac{(\bar Y_n - 0.4)\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\ge\frac{-0.2\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\right]\), 
thus \(\frac{-0.2\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{0.24}}\le z^*_{0.05}\)
and \(n\ge\left(-5 z^*_{0.05}\sqrt{0.24}\right)^2 \approx\)
```{r}
(-5*qnorm(0.05)*sqrt(0.24))^2
```   

This value of \(n\) is not large enough for the CLT. Thus, the calculations above are not justified. 
However, we can use the value \(n=17\) as an initial guess.
            
To calculate \(\Pr[\bar Y_n\ge0.2]\) exactly, not approximately, it is sufficient to note that
\(n\bar Y_n\sim B(n,0.4)\) and \(\Pr[\bar Y_n\ge0.2] = \Pr[n\bar Y_n\ge0.2n] = 1 - \Pr[n\bar Y_n < 0.2n]\).
```{r}
check.prob <- function(N){
  (1-pbinom(q=N %/% 5 + ifelse(N %% 5 == 0,-1,0), size=N, prob=0.4)) >= 0.95
}
print(first.good.N <- match(TRUE,sapply(1:20,check.prob)))
```   
The smallest value of \(n\) is \(10\). 

This difference between \(10\) and \(17\) is mostly due to the fact that the binomial distribution 
makes jumps at integer values:
```{r}
1-pbinom(0.2*17,17,0.4)
1-pbinom(0.2*16,16,0.4)
1-pbinom(0.2*11,11,0.4)
1-pbinom(0.2*10-1,10,0.4)
1-pbinom(0.2*9,9,0.4)
```

# Exercise 16
## a)
```{r}
earnings <- c(-99750, -99500, -99250, -99000, -98750, 1250)
probabilities <- c(.00183,.00186,.00189,.00191,.00193,NA)
probabilities[is.na(probabilities)] <- 1-sum(probabilities,na.rm=TRUE)
probabilities
mean.earnings <- sum(earnings*probabilities)
```   

## b)

The earnings \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) from each of \(n\) young man have the same distribution as \(X\).

However, people deaths are independent (quite often, the independence is additionally guaranteed by special clauses making insurance invalid in case of mass deaths), and the total earnings \(X_1+\cdots+X_n\) will have approximately normal distribution with mean \(n\mathbf{E} X\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}\).
Thus, the standard deviation of the total earnings grows slower than the mean of the total earnings 
(as a \(\sqrt{n}\) compared to \(n\)), 
so for a sufficiently large \(n\) the total earnings will almost surely be close to their mean.

## c)

The probability of losses is \(\Pr[X_1+\cdots+X_n < 0]\), 
so for each value of \(\alpha\) among \(0.01\), \(0.001\) and \(0.000001\)
we need to find the smallest \(n\) such that \(\Pr[X_1+\cdots+X_n < 0] \le \alpha\).

Assuming that \(n\) is large enough to use the CLT, 
\(\Pr[X_1+\cdots+X_n < 0] 
  = \Pr\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n - n\mathbf{E} X}{\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}} 
                      < \frac{- n\mathbf{E} X}{\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}}
                 \right]\).
Thus, \(\frac{- n\mathbf{E} X}{\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}} \le z^*_{\alpha}\)
and \(\sqrt{n} \ge \frac{-z^*_{\alpha}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}}{\mathbf{E} X}\).
The required values of \(n\) are
```{r}
var.earnings <- sum(earnings^2*probabilities) - mean.earnings^2
alpha <- c(0.01,0.001,0.000001)
ceiling((-qnorm(alpha)*sqrt(var.earnings)/mean.earnings)^2)
```   
All of them are more than enough for the CLT.

# Exercise 17

## a)
The UK voting population is so large, so we can consider it infinite, hence \(X\sim B(n,p)\)
(absolutely precisely, \(X\) has a hypergeometric distribution, but this precision is practically irrelevant).

For a large \(n\), the distribution of \(X\) is approximately normal with mean \(np\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\), while the distribution of \(\hat p = \frac{X}{n}\) is approximately normal with mean \(p\) 
and standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\)

## b)
We assume that \(n\) is large, so \(\hat p\sim{N}\left(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\right)\). 
\(\Pr[|\hat p - p|\le 0.02] = 0.95\), thus \(\frac{0.02\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{p(1-p)}} = z^*_{0.975}\) and \(n \ge \left(\frac{z^*_{0.975}}{0.02}\right)^2 p(1-p)\).
       
As the value of \(p\) is not known (we want to estimate it!), we need to select \(n\), which would work for any \(p\), that is, 
\(n \ge \left(\frac{z^*_{0.975}}{0.02}\right)^2 \max\limits_p \{p(1-p)\}\).

One can easily check using methods of calculus that \(\max\limits_p \{p(1-p)\}=0.25\).
Alternatively, from the plot 
```{r,fig.align='center'}
curve(x*(1-x),0,1)
```   
and the ideas of symmetry we can conclude that the largest value of \(p(1-p)\) is achieved when \(p=0.5\),
which gives \(\max\limits_p \{p(1-p)\}=0.25\).

Therefore, \(n  \ge \left(\frac{z^*_{0.975}}{0.02}\right)^2 \cdot 0.25\approx\)
```{r}
(qnorm(0.975)/0.02)^2 * 0.25
```   

This is large enough for the CLT, so the smallest sample size that guarantees the margin of error of \(2\)\% with probability \(95\)\% is \(2401\). 



# Exercise 18
The sample size is $100$,  so the distribution of the mean can be considered approximately normal. The sample mean is $72$, and the estimated standard deviation $12$ is not obtained from this sample.
```{r}
z.conf.int<-function(sample.mean,sigma,n,level=0.95){ 
  margin<-sigma*qnorm(1-(1-level)/2)/sqrt(n); 
  c(sample.mean-margin,sample.mean+margin)
}
z.conf.int(72,12,100)
```

# Exercise 19
We can calculate a $95$% confidence interval assuming that the standard deviation is $0.707$:
```{r}
water<-scan("water.csv",sep=",")
z.conf.int(mean(water),0.707,length(water))
```
The interval includes $7.6$, so the authority is probably correct.

# Exercise 20

## a)
```{r}
mu <- 3
sigma <- 3
sample.size <- 20
smpl.20 <- rnorm(sample.size,mu,sigma)
```
### (i)
```{r}
mu_hat <- mean(smpl.20)
mu_hat
```
### (ii)
The 95% confidence interval is
```{r}
z.conf.int(mu_hat,sigma,length(smpl.20))
```
The 90% confidence interval will be narrower as we are allowed to make mistakes more often and hence can be more definite in our estimate; the 99% confidence interval will be wider.
```{r}
z.conf.int(mu_hat,sigma,length(smpl.20),0.9)
z.conf.int(mu_hat,sigma,length(smpl.20),0.99)
```  
### (iii)
All three intervals above contain the true value `r mu`, though this may be different for your intervals.

## b) 
```{r fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
n.samples <- 100
samples <- rnorm(n.samples*sample.size,mu,sigma)
means <- apply(matrix(samples,ncol=sample.size),1,mean)
hist(means,freq=FALSE,main="Distribution of the Sample Mean")
```   

Let's now calculate confidence intervals and check how many of them contain the true mean:
```{r}
conf.ints.matrix <- t(sapply(means,function(x){z.conf.int(x,sigma,sample.size)}))
conf.ints <- setNames(as.data.frame(conf.ints.matrix),c("Low","High"))
conf.ints$Case <- 1:nrow(conf.ints)
does.contain.true.value <- function(interval,value){
  (interval[1] <= value) & (value <= interval[2]) 
}
conf.ints$Is.Good <- apply(conf.ints.matrix,1,does.contain.true.value,value=mu)
paste0(mean(!conf.ints$Is.Good)*100,"% of confidence intervals do not contain the true value.")
```   
```{r fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data=conf.ints) + geom_linerange(aes(x=Case,ymin=Low,ymax=High,colour=Is.Good)) + 
  scale_colour_manual(name="Confidence interval",
                      values=c("FALSE"="red","TRUE"="black"),
                      labels=c("FALSE"="does not contain true value","TRUE"="contains true value")) + 
  theme(legend.position="bottom") + 
  geom_hline(yintercept=mu,colour="green") + 
  ggtitle("Confidence Intervals and the True Value")
```    

## c) 
```{r}
sample.size <- 100
smpl.100 <- rnorm(sample.size,mu,sigma)
print(mu_hat <- mean(smpl.100))
z.conf.int(mu_hat,sigma,length(smpl.100))
z.conf.int(mu_hat,sigma,length(smpl.100),0.9)
z.conf.int(mu_hat,sigma,length(smpl.100),0.99)
```  
All three intervals are narrower than the respective intervals above for the sample size of 20.

```{r fig.align='center',fig.width=10}
samples <- rnorm(n.samples*sample.size,mu,sigma)
means <- apply(matrix(samples,ncol=sample.size),1,mean)
hist(means,freq=FALSE,main="Distribution of the Sample Mean")
conf.ints.matrix <- t(sapply(means,function(x){z.conf.int(x,sigma,sample.size)}))
conf.ints <- setNames(as.data.frame(conf.ints.matrix),c("Low","High"))
conf.ints$Case <- 1:nrow(conf.ints)
does.contain.true.value <- function(interval,value){
  (interval[1] <= value) & (value <= interval[2]) 
}
conf.ints$Is.Good <- apply(conf.ints.matrix,1,does.contain.true.value,value=mu)
paste0(mean(!conf.ints$Is.Good)*100,"% of confidence intervals do not contain the true value.")
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data=conf.ints) + geom_linerange(aes(x=Case,ymin=Low,ymax=High,colour=Is.Good)) + 
  scale_colour_manual(name="Confidence interval",
                      values=c("FALSE"="red","TRUE"="black"),
                      labels=c("FALSE"="does not contain true value","TRUE"="contains true value")) + 
  theme(legend.position="bottom") + 
  geom_hline(yintercept=mu,colour="green") + 
  ggtitle("Confidence Intervals and the True Value")
```    

Try to increase the number of samples and see what happens.
